Abjad Howse – à Montréal, ce collectif e: Abjad Howse – in Montréal, this collective is known for its game nights, stand-up comedy shows and events in Arabic. Behind this puzzle of a name is a community of Arabic-speaking artists, but also friends brought together by their love of humanity.
Parmi eux, il y a la clown, dramathérape: Among them are clown, drama therapist, artist and comedian Sandy El Bitar. Since she is currently visiting Lebanon, we took the opportunity to meet her in her hometown, Beirut. Here is the portrait of a committed artist who works for equity every day.
Il est 17 h 30, la nuit est tombée aussi: It is 5:30 p.m., and night has fallen over the Lebanese capital as quickly as the rain. Sandy is waiting for us in the basement of an upscale bar-café in Mar Mikhael, a Beirut neighbourhood that was disfigured by the explosion of August 4, 2020. The dim lighting, colourful walls, sofas and piano are a perfect match for this curious, altruistic, jack-of-all-trades artist. “I like to introduce myself as a good play partner,” she says teasingly. About to finish her master’s degree in drama therapy, she flits between projects and creations. “I have too many passions,” she says, smiling, her eyes curious.
Plusieurs de ces passions sont nées ici,: Many of these passions were born here in Lebanon, where she studied theatre. Sandy was barely 18 when she became one of the country’s six clown doctors (therapeutic clowns) working in Beirut hospitals, in 2008. “It shaped me and greatly influenced my decisions afterward,” she explains. “I wasn’t there just to give a performance, but also to help. Yes, they’re sick, but they’re still human and they can play!” adds Sandy, who brightened the days of many hospitalized people.
Un an plus tard, en 2010, Sandy arrive a: A year later, in 2010, Sandy arrived in Canada with her family, who were fleeing Lebanon’s sociopolitical situation. “I know it’s worse now, but back then, the feeling was that you couldn’t have financial security. I was 12 when I started hearing my parents talk about immigrating. We got here after I turned 19,” the artist continues. Her father had died before the departure, so she left with her mother, her two sisters and her brother to join her maternal family. “I think my mother mostly wanted to give us better chances in this world,” she confides. How did she experience her integration in Quebec? Sandy bursts out laughing, hiding her face behind her hands to show just how hard it was. “For the first two years, a part of me died,” says the therapist.
En plus de la perte d’identité, de la di: On top of the loss of identity, the difficulty of making friends, the language barrier and the values of a family pressing her to continue her studies, she learned that her “experiences in Lebanon were worth nothing,” among other reasons because professional equivalencies were not recognized. For someone who had been so proud of her work in the hospital, the shock was immense. “I’m a Lebanese woman from a religious minority and I work in comedy,” she sums up to explain her difficulties. As she lost her bearings, Sandy even went as far as erasing her Lebanese accent in English. “I talked like people from Ottawa! But later, when I got to Montréal, I told myself I would speak with my accent and my Arabic words,” she recalls proudly.
C’est ainsi qu’à l’aube de la vingtaine,: So it was that at the dawn of her twenties, Sandy settled in Aylmer, a sector of the city of Gatineau. After a first work experience on Canadian soil at the local Tim Hortons, she went from job to job and hobby to hobby. “I did jewellery repair, woodworking, hairdressing, painting on canvas and on clothing, and so on,” lists this jack-of-all-trades. Anything to put her hands, her body and her creativity to work. Nostalgic for her work in hospitals, she joined a long-term care facility and a seniors’ residence. Caring for the residents, many of them in palliative care, she discovered a raw, uninhibited world. “I loved showing these people that, even though they’re close to death, they can have good moments,” she says of the experience, which inspired a stand-up routine about the end of life. She then got involved with L’Abri d’espoir, a shelter for homeless women in Montréal, until 2019.
Parallèlement aux emplois qu’elle occupe: Alongside her jobs, Sandy began a recreation and leisure services technician program at Algonquin College in Ottawa, then studied psychology at the University of Ottawa. Today, the artist dedicates herself enormously to the community. She is a member of Abjad Howse, with whom she hosts evenings and performs stand-up, in addition to doing content creation and graphic design. The collective was born three years ago, in 2019. “We were alone, without our families nearby. We needed a moment, a space to express ourselves and practise our art. We met once a week, and the ideas came,” she remembers. Simply, as if the collective had always existed.
<strong>‍</strong>Maintenant, il ne lui: ‍Now, all she has left to do is hand in her research paper to complete her master’s degree in drama therapy at Concordia University. In spring 2022, she will return from Lebanon, where she has spent several months. She plans to continue her community activities in a small space in Montréal’s Old Port. “I also intend to practise therapy there. There will be room to explore different media: paper, objects, movement, creation,” the artist continues.
Spécialisée en dramathérapie, Sandy util: Specializing in drama therapy, Sandy uses theatre, the body and play to heal minds: “Through play, defence mechanisms slip away and fade. You can go further without causing trauma.” Beyond her practice, she devoted her thesis to humour in therapy: “I think humour has the power to foster resilience and make people more creative.” It’s an approach she also applies to herself in her stand-up routines. This path has not been without obstacles. “I’m traumatized!” she says bluntly. Coming from a “very conservative” family, Sandy had to build herself in an environment where she was muzzled. Therapy and humour are what allowed her to heal. But she has no choice but to hide this part of herself from her family: “They would disown me if they discovered certain aspects of who I am. It’s either being myself or losing my family,” the artist explains. “When are you going to stop clowning around and start your real life?” she is constantly asked.
Ce séjour au Liban est l’occasion de ren: This stay in Lebanon is a chance to reconnect with her loved ones and her country of origin after about ten years away, but also to put her experiences into perspective. The artist continues to navigate unequal environments, starting with comedy. She describes in detail the stubborn prejudice that “women aren’t funny.” While there are more women in the comedy scene in Quebec, Sandy estimates that there are fewer than ten in Lebanon. During her studies there, inappropriate remarks were frequent.
Au-delà de l’humour, elle décrit plusieu: Beyond comedy, she describes several aspects of her life as a struggle. “I don’t mean that I fight every day, but it’s true that I have to speak louder to succeed. It’s a long struggle,” says Sandy, speaking of the adversity tied to her experience as a woman, here as elsewhere: groping at university, sexualization, men repeatedly cutting in to speak, and the underrepresentation of women in the media. Careful not to compare what can’t be compared, she nonetheless believes that in Lebanon, society is more unequal for women. “Being a woman, accepting your body and your sexuality, is hard. There is a lot of fear, a lot of harassment, and little support offered to the victims of this behaviour,” the artist laments. “In Montréal, being a woman doesn’t force me to fight as much. But inequalities, sexist stereotypes and microaggressions remain. When I react intensely to something, I’m told it’s hormones,” she offers as an example, with a great deal of nuance, however, because the systems are very different. She believes it is a societal problem. “A lot of space is given to them,” she says of men. “What women do is barely represented, and people just talk about their appearance, their diet or their bodies, when there is so much to say!” She wants to see more of what women do shown, and more support offered to them. “We need to create more equity before talking about equality,” she says.
Alors que la conversation se poursuit da: As the conversation continues in this little café, Sandy’s words come to life as if by magic. Within minutes of each other, two men allow themselves to barge into our conversation, each politely interrupting the discussion to “add something.” They carry on with their monologues and go back to what they were doing without grasping the substance of our exchange.
Quelques jours plus tard, Sandy me fait: A few days later, Sandy shares her impressions with me in a voice message: “The irony of life. Y3ani [I mean], we got a concrete example of the space men take up. They didn’t know what we were talking about, but they felt entitled to share their experiences. One of them, claiming to support the cause, did it in a way that takes up space. I found it so funny!” That evening, these interruptions seemed straight out of a sketch Sandy could have written to talk about her life and the reality of women.
